summary: Steel tower 13 miles off Cape Hatteras, lit 1966 after lightships from 1897; a caisson failed in 1891; private and closed since 2001.

access.note: Privately owned and not open to the public (US Lighthouse Society record). Offshore, about 13 miles out; the structure has a helicopter pad.

facts.agency: Private owner (bought from the General Services Administration in 2012)

events.note: Caisson for a light-house on the outer shoal anchored 1 July 1891; it sank out of level and the attempt was given up.
Skeleton iron boring frame set on the shoal in May 1894 to test the site.
Act of 11 June 1896 directed part of the appropriation to a light-vessel; light-house plans stopped.
Lightship station established (USLHS); light vessels Nos. 69 and 71 built 1897-98.
Light-vessel No. 69 relieved No. 71 on station, 24 November 1898.
Light-vessel No. 69 dragged her anchor in a January gale and broke adrift; replaced on station 11 January.
August 1899 cyclone drove No. 69 from her anchorage; she was thrown ashore near Creeds Hill.
Southwest gale blew No. 71 about 1 mile off station; returned next day.
No. 71 took off the captain, his wife and crew of ten from the wrecked schooner M. D. Cressy.
Light vessel No. 71 fired upon and sunk by an enemy submarine, 6 August 1918; crew of 12 landed in boats.
Act of 4 November 1919 appropriated $450,000 for a replacement light vessel.
Station marked by light vessel No. 72, a relief vessel.
Steel skeletal tower (Texas tower) established with keepers' quarters in the structure.
Tower took over from lightship WLV-189, the last vessel on the station (USLHS list ends 1966).
Light extinguished December 2001; USLHS gives year discontinued 2001.
Federal surplus auction (GSA); sold to a private buyer for $20,000 in September 2012.

wrecks.outcome: Struck the outer Diamond Shoal and bilged, falling over on her beam ends; the passage read gives no further outcome.
Stranded on the outer Diamond Shoal; crew and master, twenty-four men, brought to shore with help from the Cape Hatteras, Creeds Hill and Big Kinnakeet stations.
Captain, his wife and ten crew taken aboard light vessel No. 71; they had been picked up by another steamer.
Driven from her anchorage in the August 1899 cyclone and thrown ashore near Creeds Hill; a wrecking agreement for $15,000 was made to haul her off.
Sunk by an enemy submarine while moored on station; her twelve men landed in boats about a mile north of Cape Hatteras Lighthouse.

corrections.why: Light extinguished December 2001 (AP) and discontinued 2001 (USLHS). USLHS also flags 'Active Aid to Navigation?: Yes', so check the current USCG Light List before applying.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record dates the station from 1966, the tower's first light. USLHS gives a lightship station established 1897 and discontinued 1966, and the tower established 1966. The story covers both: the lightships from 1897 and the tower from 1966.
USLHS gives 1897 as the start for No. 69; the Light-House Board's 1899 report says No. 71 was on station until 24 November 1898, when No. 69 relieved her. The story follows the Board's report.
USLHS and the 2012 AP report give automation in 1977; the station's own website says the Coast Guard manned it until 1979. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Rich for 1891-1918: Light-House Board, Life-Saving Service, Lighthouse Service Bulletin and Commissioner reports. Thin for the tower (1966-2026): the USLHS record, the station's website and the 2012 AP report; the NYT 1966 notice and the USCG Historian page were not read. Checked on page images: Bulletin 1913 PDF p. 46 (printed p. 94): A. T. Loss to a Virginia light vessel; C. H. Pertner to mate of No. 71. Bulletin 1914 PDF p. 3 (printed p. 99): Sidney Atherton appointed second mate of No. 71. Bulletin 1915 PDF p. 11 (printed p. 156): Sidney Atherton transferred to the tender Ivy (the OCR reads 'l Vy'); the 'Orchid' line in the same column belongs to another officer, so the earlier draft's Orchid was wrong. Commissioner fiscal 1921 scan p. 626 (printed p. 22) carries 'light vessel No. 72, which was a relief vessel'; the fiscal 1920 text is on scan p. 521. Wetherby master's letter and Formosa letter (Life-Saving Service) read as cited. The 1899 $15,000 figure comes from the same sentence as the quoted agreement; the OCR breaks it as '$15 ,000'. The Light-House Board's 1899 entry for No. 69 gives 'built in 1897-98' and the Board's 1899 note gives the cyclone as 16 and 18 August (OCR 'Auflrast 16 and 18^'). The USLHS roster (21 crew, 3 principal keepers) is cited as printed; USLHS asks that each keeper be confirmed in a primary record before a story names them, and this story names only the three principal keepers. The record's 'active' status (USLHS: Active Aid to Navigation: Yes) conflicts with the 2001 discontinuance; the Light List should settle it. The 1966 tower record (USLHS) gives automation in 1977; the station's website gives manned until 1979 and automation in 1979. Both are in the story. The Commissioner's fiscal 1920 report at scan p. 539 (printed p. 41) reads 'act of November 1, 1919' for the same $450,000 light vessel; the OCR may misread the day, and the story follows the 4 November date given at scans 520, 522 and 626. Lightship crews from the Bulletin are only the officers named in notices; no crew list was found.
